The Nernst effect, a thermoelectric conversion mech-
anism that transforms thermal gradients into transverse
electrical signals, holds significant promise for applica-
tions in waste heat recovery and highly sensitive thermal
sensors [1–6]. In conventional ferromagnetic systems, the
anomalous Nernst thermopower (SxAy) empirically scales
with the magnetization SxAy = QSµ0M, in which QS is
anomalous Nernst coefficient and ranges from 0.05 to
1 µVK−1T−1 for trivial ferromagnets. Recent explo-
rations of magnetic topological quantum materials have
revealed that their non-zero Berry curvature can generate
a giant anomalous Nernst effect (ANE) [7–14].

stems from the Berry curvature—an intrinsic property
of the electronic band structure dictated by magnetic-
ordering-induced time-reversal symmetry breaking and
spin-orbit coupling—which demonstrates significant tem-
perature dependence.[15–17]. The SxAy of Co3Sn2S2
peaks at ∼2.9 µV/K at 80 K but diminishes sharply to
∼0.13 µV/K at 300 K [9]. Similarly, Mn3Sn exhibits a
maximum SxAy of ∼0.6 µV/K at 160 K, which declines
to ∼0.37 µV/K at 300 K [10]. In contrast, TbMn6Sn6
demonstrates enhanced performance at elevated temper-
atures, achieving SxAy∼ 2.15 µV/K at 300 K and fur-
ther increasing to ∼2.4 µV/K at 320 K [18]. Partic-
ularly noteworthy are Heusler alloys such as Co2MnGa,
which have emerged as leading candidates for large room-
temperature ANE [19–22]. Xu et al. reported a giant
ANE thermopower of approximately 8 µV/K at 300 K in
Co2MnGa single crystals [19]. Within the family of RCo5
(R
= Lanthanum rare earth ) compounds, which posses

a crystal structure analogous to LaCo5, an ANE ther-
mopower of 3.1 µV/K at 300 K was reported in SmCo5
[23]. These examples highlight the ongoing efforts and
diverse material platforms being explored for enhancing
ANE, especially at room temperatures.
In our prior work, we observed a large Berry
curvature-driven room-temperature anomalous Nernst
thermopower (4.6 µV/K at 300 K) in LaCo5 single
crystals—a kagome and honeycomb magnet with a high
Curie temperature (TC = 840 K) [26, 27]. First-principles
calculations revealed a dense distribution of Weyl points
near the Fermi level, suggesting a strong Berry curva-
ture contribution [26]. To further optimize the ANE, in
this work, we engineered Pr-doped LaCo5 (La1−xPrxCo5,
x = 0.09, 0.21, 0.45) by introducing chemical pressure via
partial Pr-for-La substitution. Crucially, this strategy

suggests the persistence of robust ferromagnetic ordering
at temperatures exceeding room temperature. The nar-
row hysteresis loops indicate weak soft ferromagnetism
dominated by domain dynamics [28].
Figures 3(a, b) show schematic illustrations of the mea-
surement configurations for the AHE and the ANE, re-
spectively. The test samples were cut into a long strip
shape with a thickness of approximately 0.1 mm. To
establish a thermal gradient for the thermoelectric mea-
surements, one end of the sample was attached to a 1 kΩ
chip resistor (heater) and the other end to a heat sink.
This setup created a longitudinal temperature gradient
(−∇T ∼ 0.4 - 1.0 K/mm) along the x-direction of the
sample as shown in Fig. 3(b). Temperatures at two points
along the sample length were monitored using thermo-
couples to determine the temperature gradient. The two
junctions of this thermocouple were carefully placed in
good thermal contact (via thermal grease, ensuring elec-
trical insulation) with the side of the sample, aligned
along its length and separated by a precisely measured
distance. High-precision Keithley 2182A Nanovoltmeter
was used to collect the voltage difference. The Nernst
and Hall signals were measured at both positive and neg-
ative magnetic field polarities, and the difference of the
two polarities was deduced to remove the longitudinal
contribution from the voltage probe misalignment.
The Pr-doped systems exhibit giant AHE character-
istics, as shown in Figs. 3 (c,d). By linearly extrap-
olating the field-dependent ρyx(B) data from the satu-
ration regime to zero field, the ρAyx was obtained. For
La0.91Pr0.09Co5, the anomalous Hall resistivity (ρAyx)
reaches ∼1.15 µΩ · cm at 10 K, decreasing to ∼0.95
µΩ · cm at 300 K. In La0.79Pr0.21Co5, the anoma-
lous Hall resistivity (ρAyx) reaches ∼1.00 µΩ · cm at 10
K, decreasing to ∼0.78 µΩ · cm at 300 K. Similarly,
the ρAyx in La0.55Pr0.45Co5 slightly decreases from ρAyx
∼1.51 µΩ · cm at 10 K to ∼1.32 µΩ · cm at 300 K.
The anomalous Hall conductivity (AHC), calculated via
σxAy ≈ ρAyx/ρ2xx, reveals critical doping effects: at 10
K, La0.91Pr0.09Co5 achieves σxAy ≈ 635 Ω−1cm−1, ex-
ceeding both the La0.55Pr0.45Co5 (∼375 Ω−1cm−1) and
La0.79Pr0.21Co5 (∼535 Ω−1cm−1). Room-temperature
σxAy values converge to ∼145 Ω−1cm−1 for both x =
0.21 and 0.45 systems—a 3 times enhancement over
LaCo5 (∼50 Ω−1cm−1). In La0.91Pr0.09Co5, the room-
temperature AHC is about 110 Ω−1cm−1. Given the
large number of Weyl points near the Fermi energy in
the parent material LaCo5, the variation in AHC could
be attributed to the shift in the Fermi energy induced by
Pr doping, which alters the Berry curvature integral over
the entire Brillouin zone [26].
To further investigate the effect of Fermi level modifi-
cation suggested by the AHC evolution under Pr doping,
we conducted systematic ANE measurements—a critical
probe of Berry curvature distribution near the Fermi sur-
face [15, 25], as the intrinsic ANE primarily originates

sible states. As shown in Figs. 4(a-c), the large ANE
is observed in all of the three compounds, in which the
SyAx increase with the increasing temperature and reach a
maximum of about 4.3 µV/K for x = 0.09, 4.1 µV/K for
x = 0.29, and 6.5 µV/K for x = 0.45, respectively. The
value of SyAx was determined by linearly extrapolating the
field-dependent Syx(B) data from the saturation regime
to zero field. To further study the origin of the ANE, the
anomalous Nernst conductivity (αyAx) is obtained by Eq.
(1) and displayed in Figs. 4(d-f). At low temperature,
the αyAx induced by the Berry curvature exhibits a linear
behavior with temperature, α y A x = −π2 3 k |e B 2 | T (∂ ∂ σ E yx ) E=EF ,
following the Mott relation [15, 29]. As shown in Figs.
4(g-i), the αyAx of these three compounds exhibit a lin-
ear temperature dependence below 160 K, indicating the
ANE in these three compounds stem from the intrinsic
Berry curvature mechanism [30]. Above 160 K, the αyAx
deviates from the linear relationship similar to the par-
ent compound LaCo5 [26]. While the lattice parameters
in this system evolve monotonically with increasing Pr
doping concentration, the anomalous Nernst signal SyAx
exhibits non-monotonic behavior. This discrepancy may
originate from the dense distribution of Weyl nodes near
the Fermi level [26], where even slight shifts in Fermi
energy can lead to a nonlinear response in the Berry cur-
vature. Such behavior is commonly observed in doped
topological magnets, a representative example is found
in In- and Ni-doped Co3Sn2S2 films [31].
The room-temperature ANE holds particular signif-
icance for practical applications. Figure 5 compares
the SyAx of LaCo5-based materials with representa-
tive magnetic topological counterparts at 300 K, along
with their respective peak-effect temperatures. Cur-
rent benchmark kagome systems typically exhibit room-
temperature SyAx typically below 6 µV/K, whereas our
optimized La0.55Pr0.45Co5 achieves 6.5 µV/K, which ex-
hibits a ∼40 % enhancement compared with the parent
material LaCo5. In addition, given the ultrahigh Curie
temperature (TC = 840 K) of the parent LaCo5 and the
positive temperature coefficient of SyAx in La1−xPrxCo5
(x = 0.09, 0.21, 0.45), these systems exhibit promis-

anomalus Nernst thermopower 6.5 µV/K, which is

high Curie temperature and exhibits a positive SyAx-T
correlation, suggesting further performance gains at
elevated temperatures. This work establishes rare-earth
doping as a scalable strategy. The synergy of high TC,
temperature-resilient ANE, and tunable Berry curvature

technologies and high-efficiency thermal sensing devices.
